terms.grammar: adjective, plural of multus; comparative plūrēs, superlative plūrimī
evidence: Cic. Fam. 5.17.3: multī fortissimī virī (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: With a second adjective Latin joins the two with et: multae et magnae contentiōnēs, many great contests (Cic., Lewis & Short). As nouns, multī are many people and multa many things.

evidence: Cic. Leg. 3.31: imitātōrēs; Caes. B.C. 3.43: collēs (Lewis & Short)

terms.comment: The superlative of multī: “very many” as well as “most”.

evidence: Tac. Agr. 17: cīvitās numerōsissima prōvinciae tōtīus (Lewis & Short)
Plin. Ep. 4.15.4: cōpiōsa et numerōsa domus (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Post-Augustan in this sense (Tacitus, the Plinies, Martial). In Cicero and Ovid numerōsus means rhythmical, in time (Lewis & Short); classical prose says multī, or frequēns of a crowded place.

phrases.latin: vērumque illud est quod dīcitur, multōs modiōs salis simul edendōs esse, ut amīcitiae mūnus explētum sit
phrases.english: and the saying is true, that many bushels of salt must be eaten together before the duty of friendship is done

phrases.latin: gallīnās multās et ōva utī habeat
phrases.english: let her keep many hens, and eggs

sources: Lewis & Short: multus · Lewis & Short: permultus
